sections.h2: Who sells houses in Harrisburg, PA, and why?
sections.html:
Harrisburg is a state capital where most homes are rented, prices are modest and many sellers are landlords or heirs. Census figures show 50,522 people in the 2025 estimate and 22,137 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey.

Just 36.6 percent of occupied homes are lived in by their owners. A typical owned home is worth $124,200, rent runs $1,062, and a household earns a median $48,099, with 30.5 percent of residents below the poverty line. About one adult in four, 25.9 percent, holds a bachelor's degree.

These figures shape a sale. Investors who price a house by its rent roll are common buyers, and lenders can be wary of a property that needs work. A vacant or tenant-occupied Harrisburg house may suit a buyer who takes it as it stands.

sections.h2: What is the layout of Harrisburg?
sections.html:
Harrisburg sits on the east bank of the Susquehanna River and is the seat of Dauphin County and the capital of Pennsylvania. Its footprint is 8.1 square miles of land plus 3.3 of water, which makes it the third smallest U.S. state capital by land area.

  • Paxton Creek empties into the Susquehanna inside the city, and the river forms the line between Dauphin and Cumberland counties.
  • Downtown holds the State Capitol complex, and there are more than a dozen neighborhoods and historic districts around it.
  • Six municipal historic districts, several national historic districts and architectural conservation overlays guide new work in older blocks.

Be careful with addresses. Several nearby townships, including Lower Paxton and Middle Paxton, use Harrisburg as their mailing name even though they sit outside city limits and follow their own codes. Check whether your parcel is inside the city before you read any rule below.

sections.h2: What does the local economy mean for a Harrisburg house sale?
sections.html:
Government jobs keep the Harrisburg market steady even when prices are low. The Region Economic Development Corporation lists the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania as the area's largest employer at 21,885 people, followed by the federal government with about 18,000. Health care, Giant Food Stores, the Hershey companies and TE Connectivity round out the top ten regional employers.

The city's history explains its housing stock. The Pennsylvania Canal and then the Pennsylvania Railroad made Harrisburg one of the more industrial cities in the Northeast in the 1800s, and the population fell by nearly half between 1950 and 2000. Many blocks therefore hold older rowhouses and brick twins that need updates. The annual Pennsylvania Farm Show, held in Harrisburg each January since 1917, brings visitors every winter.

sections.h2: Which roads and transit connect Harrisburg homes to the region?
sections.html:
Interstate 83 runs through the middle of the city and meets Interstate 81 to the north. Interstate 76, the Pennsylvania Turnpike, passes south of town, and Interstate 283 links the turnpike and I-83 southeast of the city. U.S. 22 crosses the northern part of the city, and Route 230 follows Cameron Street.

Harrisburg International Airport sits southeast of the city in Middletown and serves about 1.2 million travelers a year. Capital Area Transit runs local bus service, and the city also has rail and intercity bus connections. Workers in the city spend an average of 20.1 minutes getting to their jobs.

sections.h2: What permits and codes apply to repairs in Harrisburg?
sections.html:
The city's Bureau of Codes handles building permits, trade licenses, rental registration and property complaints, and you can reach it at 717-255-6553. Harrisburg follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, with the 2021 international code editions in force from January 1, 2026.

  • Permits are required for roofing, fences, sheds, decks, replacement windows and doors, any structural work, new furnaces and any work above $1,000.
  • Residential permit applications must be decided within 15 business days, or 5 days if stamped by a licensed design professional. Historic Review Board review adds time.
  • A building permit expires after 6 months if work is not continuous.
  • Electricians and plumbers must hold a city license, and every contractor needs a city business privilege license.
  • The Bureau Health Officer enforces lead-based paint hazard rules for residential structures.

If you did work in the past without a permit, call the Bureau before you list. That way you know what is open on the property before a buyer asks.

sections.h2: What must a buyer do with a Harrisburg rental or condemned house?
sections.html:
A buyer of a Harrisburg rental or condemned house takes on city deadlines from the day of recording. The Bureau of Codes says a non-condemned rental must be registered within 10 days of purchase, and a condemned property needs permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase.

The program under Ordinance 1-2017 also requires an inspection at least once every five years, taxes and utilities to be current before a unit can be rented, and a local managing agent when the owner lives more than 50 miles away. The annual landlord license is separate and runs through the Bureau of Licensing, Taxation and Central Support at 717-255-6513.

If you sell a tenant-occupied house, tell the buyer which of these items are paid up.

sections.h2: How does transfer tax work when you sell in Dauphin County?
sections.html:
In Dauphin County the Recorder of Deeds takes the deed and collects the transfer tax. The commonwealth charges 1 percent of the property's value, and a local share goes to school districts and municipalities. The Department of Revenue holds grantor and grantee jointly liable, so have your title company show the split on the closing statement.

Heirs who receive a house through a will, or with none, owe no transfer tax on that inheritance. Their own later sale is a fresh transfer. The Dauphin County valuation factor published by the revenue department is 2.61 for deeds accepted in the year that began July 1, 2026.

The recorder's fee calculators add that a deed for token consideration between tax-exempt parties carries no transfer tax, and checks go to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

sections.h2: Which way should I sell a Harrisburg house?
sections.html:
Harrisburg sellers generally pick from three paths.

  • A listing suits a house in decent shape and an owner who can wait for a buyer with loan approval.
  • Going without an agent trims the listing fee, though showings, forms and bargaining fall to you.
  • A cash offer fits a vacant, damaged, inherited or rented property, with the closing date up to you.

Weigh what you would keep after repairs, carrying costs and fees on each path, not the offer alone.

faqs.q: Can a Harrisburg house be sold with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer steps into the lease, and one who keeps renting must register the unit with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days of purchase. Hand over your lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a condemned Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: Yes. The Bureau of Codes says the new owner must secure permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase, so buyers who can handle repairs are the usual fit.

faqs.q: Is transfer tax due when I inherit a Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: No. State revenue rules treat inheritance transfers, with or without a will, as exempt. Your later sale to a buyer carries the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about permits on a Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: The Bureau of Codes, at 717-255-6553, handles permits and inspections. The city lists roofing, windows, decks, sheds and any job above $1,000 among the work that needs one.

faqs.q: Is my Harrisburg mailing address inside the city?
faqs.a: Not always. Lower Paxton, Middle Paxton and other nearby townships carry a Harrisburg mailing name but are separate municipalities with their own codes. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.
